I’ve just finished the three‑player WebSocket protocol test and it passed all 13 checks, confirming that the server‑side fixes for spawning, leave handling, and tag mechanics are solid. The next logical step is to verify the full client‑side experience with three real browsers, because the user asked to “ensure smooth gameplay and all features work properly, assume three players which you will create.” The WS test only covered deterministic logic and network messages; I still need to exercise the UI, rendering performance, in‑game interactions, studio collaboration, chat, friends system, and leave handling under realistic conditions.

To do this I’ll write an automated Playwright script that launches three Chromium instances (headless, using the system Chrome for speed) and drives them through the entire game flow. The script should:
1. Register three distinct accounts (randomized usernames to avoid collisions) and log them in.
2. Measure FPS on each client to confirm rendering stays above a minimal threshold (e.g., >10 FPS) even when using SwiftShader.
3. Join all three players into the same “Tower of Bother” obby and verify the leaderboard shows three entries on every client.
4. Perform movement inputs for each player and capture a screenshot from the third player to prove both peers’ avatars are visible.
5. Test bi‑directional chat by sending messages from two different players and confirming they appear on all three clients.
6. Trigger a death and respawn sequence (Space + R) and verify the UI messages and respawn timing.
7. Have one player leave and ensure the scoreboard updates to two entries on the remaining clients.
8. Open the studio editor simultaneously for all three, add collaborators via API, and confirm each sees the other two editor presence chips.
9. Place different parts concurrently, then check via the game API that all edits persisted (partCount should reflect the three new parts plus the original ones).
10. Delete a part from the third editor and verify the deletion syncs and persists.
11. Test studio team chat similarly to in‑game chat.
12. Finally, exercise the friends system: send friend requests from the first player to the other two, accept them via UI, verify the “Playing” status appears, and use the “Join” button to have the first player jump into the friend’s game, confirming they land in the same lobby.

All of these steps should be wrapped in a test harness that logs pass/fail counts, captures any console or page errors, takes a few screenshots for visual verification, and exits with a non‑zero code if any check fails. The script will be saved to a temporary location (`/tmp/glint-3p-ui.js`) so I can run it immediately after creation.

I need to construct the full JavaScript content for this Playwright test, ensuring all required modules are imported (`chromium` from Playwright, `fs` for any file ops), constants (`BASE`, `SHOTS`), helper functions (`signup`, `measureFPS`), and the async IIFE that orchestrates the scenario. The code must match the style of the previous WS test and include detailed console logs and the `ok` helper for reporting. I’ll embed the random suffix generation for usernames, set up the browser launch options (`headless: true`, `executablePath: '/usr/bin/google-chrome'`, `args: ['--enable-unsafe-swiftshader']`), and handle cookies for authenticated API calls.

Given all this, the appropriate next action is to write this script to `/tmp/glint-3p-ui.js` with the exact content I’ve outlined. This will allow me to run the UI test next and complete the verification of smooth gameplay across three players.
